posts.body_html: In full force, photos taken 5/6/19:

Some more various select clones of S. flava var. rubricporpora Liberty Co, FL. Pics taken 6/18/19:


Look at that color...WOW!


I don't know of a single clone of rubricorpora from Liberty Co, FL that doesn't have the lid color up as the trap ages. That pristine, yellow lid you see all the time is from freshly opened traps. here's a typical trap's lid after it has aged a bit:

Some new pics, taken 6/25/19. First up, a pretty dark one (to the right):



Regarding lid color, after growing hundreds of different clones from Liberty Co, FL, it seems I haven't come across a single one that maintains that solid yellow top. Almost all of them open up with yellow lids, but as the trap ages, red pigments tend to infiltrate, here's what I'm talking about-old, aged trap to the left, newly open trap to the right:


Not the best pic, but you can see a lot of older lids in this pic, notice the production of red anthocyanins:


Here's another good example, a middle aged trap and an older trap, these are from the same exact plant. not all traps have their lids turn this red:


Some clones start off with pretty red lids though:

Looks pretty beautiful to me:

posts.body_html:
Here's S. flava var. rubricorpora (new genetics) Liberty Co, FL. Grew out several hundred seedlings, narrowed it down to 29 individuals that stood out from the rest, but truth be told, there might still be more in the batch to select out. These were selected for the ease by which they color up relative to the rest of the seedlings. Surprisingly, a few of these are dark clones that appear to be performing for the first time this year, will probably do a write up on each stand out individual once they fully color up. Just like the atropurpureas, the darker clones don't fully color up out here until the traps have aged for a while. There's also one individual with an unusually gigantic lid, will do a write up soon, so stay tuned! These rubricorpora traps were late to emerge because of our unusually cool weather this year, we're maybe 2-3 weeks behind previous years.

The divisions being offered now come from these plants!

Pics taken 5/5/20 and probably on some other days:

Did a massive grow out a few years ago, culled all the ones that didn't look great or grow strong, and kept only the best! Figured it's worth documenting these photos on this thread, these are seedlings from crossing my best rubricorpora clones with each other! These are pictures from last season, this coming spring I think it's going to be pretty stunning, I guess we'll see what happens!


this is how you find the best of the best, grow out a Ef TON!


The very worse one is absolutely great, thanks to selective pressure and heavy culling:

posts.body_html:
update on the pheno hunt, pics taken 5/25/23. What isn't visible are the hundreds of seedlings that were culled early on: maybe 40% of all the seedlings were rugeliis, "watered down rubricorporas," and ornatas. I only kept the individuals with dark red bodies, since the goal here is to find atropurpureas.

Ran out of time this season, these really needed to be transplanted last winter, but it should be all good, they'll get spaced this coming dormancy period. Pics taken 5/25/23:



It takes multiple years to find all the atros, they don't always color up right away. Interestingly, not all the ones I selected out last season are "atro'ing" right now, probably because they need to be left undisturbed to reach their fullest color potential. This is true with pretty much all atro clones:

posts.body_html:
some updated pics! up till this point, you've only seen plants that were selected for red bodies/yellow tops. In reality, this variant isn't stable and it takes quite a bit of selective pressure and selective breeding, as well as huge numbers of seedlings, to get a lot of red individuals!

Here's what they look like, unselected. notice many are "hard to color up" and/or not rubricorpora at all!


However, some of them are nice!


You really have to breed with superior parents to get a higher frequency of red bodied offspring. Generally speaking, if you take random plants, this is what the usual result is:



And here's the result of selective breeding AND intense selective pressure! You're only seeing about a third of the plants that were started, the rest were culled because they didn't make the cut! I started over a 1000 seedlings to yield several hundred that look like this!
